#5260. Strategy adds 811 Bitcoin as leverage falls to 3% – Room for bigger buys?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Strategy is continuing to increase the size of its Bitcoin [BTC] treasury. This comes with the latest addition of 811 BTC during the last week of October and the first week of November.

This purchase took its total holdings to 849,327 Bitcoins. Strategy also purchased $208 million of STRC. This demonstrated additional utilization of the company’s capital structure to fund both shareholder and treasury-related activities.

It’s worth noting that Strategy still holds $4.9 billion in USD, providing liquidity for future purchases and financial obligations.

By controlling over 4% of the total supply of Bitcoin in circulation today, Strategy is limiting the number of coins available for purchase by all market participants.

While Strategy may continue to add to its existing inventory of BTC and create greater institutional demand for them. Moreover, it will also have an increasing degree of sensitivity to changes in their value due to its increased exposure.

Strategy’s declining leverage demonstrates the changing financial condition of Strategy as its Bitcoin treasury has grown. At the beginning of January 2023, the strategy’s overall leverage was approximately 108%.

As such, Strategy was then more sensitive to its obligation to repay debt compared to its current reserves.

However, by November, Strategy’s overall leverage had declined to just 3%. Even though Strategy held significantly more Bitcoin at that time, the decline in leverage is a reflection of a much healthier balance sheet on the part of Strategy.

These resources give it more room to manage debt and fund operations without immediately selling Bitcoin.

Thus, Strategy will be able to accumulate Bitcoin through the entire range of prices. This includes down markets and maintaining the demand for Bitcoin among institutions while minimizing its own exposure to price fluctuations.

Strategy has continued to develop its treasury strategy. However, safety of custody for institutional investors is a major component of increasing investor demand.

Institutional investors that have large holdings of Bitcoins need to be able to protect their investments by taking measures to avoid loss through theft or unauthorized transactions.

Many institutional investors now use cold storage systems and multi-signature wallet structures. The multi-signature system requires consent of more than two parties before any transaction can occur.

Safety and transparency of custody and reporting will be key in maintaining the confidence of institutional investors in Bitcoin. Those elements could also be used to help sustain the interest of institutional investors regardless of the current market conditions.

Strategy currently holds 849,327 BTC in its treasury, representing more than 4% of all the Bitcoins that exist.

Strategy cut leverage to 3%, but custody risks could threaten institutional demand.

A Hyperliquid whale holds a $44 million long on 35 million XRP, nearly 80% of large-wallet XRP longs, with liquidation at $0.9626, about 23% below the current price.

Crypto liquidations reached $386.42 million in 24 hours, 88% of them longs, led by Bitcoin ($100.74 million) and Ethereum ($49.31 million).

US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $398.62 million in net daily outflows, led by Fidelity’s FBTC ($164 million), while 44,857 ETH left spot Ethereum ETFs.

Binance posted a record $15.4 billion weekly net outflow following a $6.3 billion hack the FBI attributed to North Korea.

This week’s key US triggers are the midterm elections and JOLTS (Tuesday), ISM services (Wednesday), the Fed balance sheet (Thursday) and Nonfarm Payrolls (Friday).

The crypto market greeted Tuesday morning, November 3, with a massive wave of margin position closures. Over the past 24 hours, the positions of 94,997 traders were forcibly liquidated for a total of $386.42 million, with 88% of all losses ($339.92 million) falling on long contracts, while Bitcoin ($100.74 million) and Ethereum ($49.31 million) led in liquidation volume as per CoinGlass.

A strong bearish skew persists in the US spot ETF sector: the net daily outflow from BTC funds amounted to $398.62 million, with the main blow falling on the Fidelity fund (FBTC), which saw $164 million leave. Over the day, 44,857 ETH were withdrawn from spot Ethereum ETFs. The combined assets under management (AUM) of all crypto ETFs stand at $95.83 billion as per SoSoValue.

The current daily outflow has spread across the entire line of exchange-traded products: SOL funds lost 129.19 thousand coins, outflows from XRP products amounted to 128.54 thousand tokens, and the specialized HYPE and ZEC funds shed 85.07 thousand and 13.53 thousand coins, respectively. Major operators are preemptively pulling liquidity out of volatile instruments ahead of the US midterm elections.

Amid the decline in market capitalization, a sharp split among participants has emerged: while retail investors are locking in losses en masse and most whales are betting on a decline, some large on-chain operators are opening aggressive counter-trend positions on decentralized exchanges.

The main event of the morning session was the actions of an unknown major player on the Hyperliquid platform, who, despite the overall market decline (NEAR dropped to $3.79, BNB to $697.67), stubbornly holds an XRP long worth tens of millions of dollars, turning the contract into the main barometer of local altcoin resilience.

The decentralized futures platform Hyperliquid is currently accumulating peak institutional volumes. At the same time, on-chain analytics of top wallets with balances of $1 million or more shows a strong bearish skew in open interest.

Of these wallets' total open positions of $4.5 billion, short contracts (shorts) account for $3.08 billion. Their long volume is limited to a modest $1.46 billion.

Leviathan addresses with positions of $50 million or more are almost unanimously betting on a further market decline. Against this grim backdrop, the long position of wallet '0x31b1ecf848443472e34d204a134812d86ab01434' remains the largest and riskiest counter-trend position in the system.

The whale holds 35.03 million XRP tokens. The notional value of the open position is $44.05 million at 10x Cross leverage.

The average entry price is $1.1298. At the peak of the morning momentum, the whale's unrealized profit exceeded $4.47 million, which amounts to more than 101% net return on the margin capital invested.

At the same time, the account's overall result is far from ideal: due to overall asset volatility, this wallet's net PnL over the past 30 days has fallen by $8.45 million.

The critical threshold in this whole story remains the forced liquidation price. The automatic position closure threshold sits at $0.9626.

The current XRP market price of around $1.2558 leaves the trader a buffer of about 23% to the liquidation point.

Large wallets' XRP positions on Hyperliquid are also skewed toward the bears. Against long positions of $55.70 million stands a massive wall of shorts worth $80.93 million. Nearly 80% of these longs belong to a single whale.

This morning's news backdrop points to a massive and painful restructuring of the entire market infrastructure. The central theme remains a severe liquidity crisis on centralized exchanges.

$6.3 billion Binance hack and the FBI's position: The agency officially attributed the attack to North Korean state cyber units. An analysis by lawyers at Reed Smith and Lathrop GPM showed that the exchange's insurance policies will not cover the damage. Standard D&O insurance protects only top management, while war exclusion clauses fully rule out payouts in the event of cyberwarfare waged by foreign states.

Record outflow of $15.4 billion: The weekly net capital outflow from Binance hit an all-time high. This volume exceeds the individual reserves of Bybit or Bitfinex and surpasses the combined balance of Gate, Bitget and KuCoin, which keeps the price of BNB at local lows.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao's loud statements about rising risks to the financial system from automated AI-powered cyberattacks came amid the incident at the exchange he created, which showed the ineffectiveness of classic defense mechanisms against coordinated cyber operations. Zhao stressed that commercial banks, due to outdated IT architecture, are more vulnerable than crypto platforms.

Against this backdrop, decentralized protocols are confidently expanding their institutional presence. Hyperliquid's annual revenue has reached $713 million, and trading volume in perpetuals on stocks and commodities via HIP-3 has exceeded $500 billion. Building on these technologies, the operator of the New York Stock Exchange (ICE) and Kraken are already preparing to launch regulated futures in the US with White House support.

Meanwhile, serious changes are also taking place at the level of the largest L1 ecosystems. House of Stake (NEAR Protocol) participants approved the deflationary initiative HSP-029 with 99.96% of the vote, reducing annual emissions from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. Daily issuance of new tokens is being cut from 89,500 to 57,300, while amid the general market decline the asset briefly dropped to $3.79.

Skepticism is meanwhile growing in the Ripple camp: the company reports that issuance of its dollar token RLUSD has surpassed $1 billion through partnerships with trust banks, but XRP holders are voicing open dissatisfaction. RLUSD is a centralized asset subject to freezing under US law, while XRP's decentralized status is not yet reflected in its market valuation.

At the same time, the Ethereum Foundation launched a platform for using the network as digital public infrastructure (DPI) for governments. Case studies on digital identity in Bhutan and confidential humanitarian aid systems have been published. At Devcon 8 in Mumbai, Vitalik Buterin called for developing verifiable code to minimize dependence on closed software and AI systems.

In the coming sessions, capital flows in the crypto market will be largely determined by external macroeconomic and political triggers. Investors and market makers need to keep the following critical factors in focus:

US Congressional midterm elections: The main political factor of this Tuesday, forcing large funds to preemptively close margin positions, cut leverage and hedge risks ahead of a change in the regulatory landscape.

Official JOLTS labor market report: Tuesday's release of job openings data will determine the short-term dynamics of the US dollar index and directly affect liquidity in high-risk assets.

ISM non-manufacturing business activity indices: Wednesday's statistics will highlight the real state of the US economy and shape the medium-term sentiment of major futures market operators.

Fed balance sheet on Thursday and Friday's Nonfarm Payrolls report: The key macroeconomic triggers of the week, which will lock in the final direction of capital flows through the end of the month.

Built by a team with experience scaling a leading DeFi lending protocol, Onlend aims to make it easier for fintechs, asset managers, curators, and asset issuers to build and operate their own lending products.

Onlend has publicly unveiled its decentralised infrastructure platform designed to let anyone create, launch, and operate their own onchain lending applications without building the underlying technology from scratch.

The project is entering a market with considerable room for expansion. Global debt surpassed $350 trillion in early 2026, according to the Institute of International Finance, while active loans across DeFi protocols currently stand at approximately $33 billion, according to DefiLlama. Although the figures measure different markets, they illustrate the relatively small scale of onchain lending today.

At the same time, the infrastructure supporting onchain financial activity continues to expand. The stablecoin market has grown beyond $300 billion, while the value of tokenized real-world assets has reached approximately $39 billion, creating new opportunities for lending products built around these assets.

However, launching such products remains challenging. Existing lending protocols offer established markets but can limit how teams configure and operate their lending use cases. Building custom infrastructure, meanwhile, requires significant engineering resources and development time.

Onlend addresses this gap with a permissionless, no-code platform that allows anyone to launch lending applications tailored to their own use-cases, users, and operational requirements.

Through Onlend, builders can configure supported assets (with multi-collateral and multi-borrow optionality), collateral parameters, interest-rate models, price oracles, liquidation mechanisms, fees, and administrative permissions. Applications can operate with open or restricted access, use a customizable white-label interface, and remain actively managed or operate under immutable rules.

One of its main technical differentiators is support for advanced interest-rate models beyond traditional utilization-based curves. These include fixed rates, rates linked to external benchmarks such as staking yields, and targeted rates for specific borrowers.

The flexibility opens several potential applications across financial services.

For fintechs and neobanks, Onlend provides a way to introduce collateral-backed borrowing directly into their existing consumer applications, adding lending functionality without developing the feature from the ground up, nor relying on rigid third-party protocols.

Asset managers and curators can create and manage lending markets aligned with their strategies, retain control over market configurations, and capture revenue through the markets they operate.

Tokenized real-world asset issuers can establish dedicated lending markets using their assets as collateral, while stablecoin issuers, liquid staking protocols, and other DeFi projects can develop lending products tailored to their ecosystems.

Designed for the emerging agentic economy, where AI agents can autonomously lend and borrow capital to finance their operations.

The approach differs from established lending protocols such as Aave, where introducing new assets into governed markets involves an approval process, and Morpho, which enables permissionless market creation but uses immutable market parameters. Onlend combines permissionless application creation with broader customization, ongoing management options, and branded interfaces.

Behind the project is a team with experience at Flowdesk, MEV Capital, and Folks Finance. Its members have previously helped scale the lending protocol to more than $400 million in peak total value locked and $13 billion in cumulative deposits volume.

With initial testnet deployments targeted for Q4 2026, Onlend is positioning itself as infrastructure for a new generation of lending applications, where teams can control their financial products rather than depend entirely on existing lending markets.

More information is available at onlend.io, and official X and Linkedin profiles.

#5255. Binance hack: Fake job assignment helped attackers reach wallet systems, exchange says

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Binance says a fake recruitment assignment helped attackers gain access to employee computers before the October 29 hack. Its initial findings describe a campaign that eventually reached an internal service used to authorize wallet transactions, affecting approximately $6.34 billion in assets.

The November 3 update expands Binance’s earlier account of a compromised engineer’s laptop. It also explains why suspending withdrawals failed to stop every transfer: attackers had established permissions on Ethereum that required separate action to revoke.

According to Binance, a software engineer was approached through a legitimate job-search platform in September. Someone posing as a project director arranged interviews with a supposed HR representative and the CEO of a fictitious company.

Near the end of the second interview, the engineer was asked to download a coding assignment onto a work computer.

Binance says the assignment contained malicious software that ran during setup. It replaced part of a legitimate development tool and connected to an attacker-controlled server, escaping detection by the device’s security tools at the time.

The exchange also disclosed an earlier June incident involving a tampered software installation downloaded by another engineer. Binance says it replaced that device and changed related credentials, although the incident exposed information about its wallet infrastructure team.

On October 20, the attackers used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain control of two colleagues’ computers, Binance said.

They discovered a credential allowing software deployment within the wallet infrastructure. On October 29, they used the stolen access to deploy software and launch the theft.

The attackers reached Binance’s wallet-signing service, enabling transfers outside the normal withdrawal process.

On Ethereum, they also used EIP-7702, a feature allowing a wallet to delegate certain functions to software. That permission let attacker-controlled code continue moving assets after Binance suspended withdrawals.

Binance says its wallet’s security design complicated emergency revocation. The team developed a specialized procedure and cleared the delegation at 00:10 UTC on October 30.

Binance says it has rebuilt affected wallet systems and its internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, and disabled related credentials.

It reports approximately $2.85 billion frozen or intercepted, with the amount subject to reconciliation and changing prices.

The company says it has reserved more than enough funds to cover the loss and is purchasing outstanding affected assets. Independent security firms will review its initial findings as the investigation continues.

#5253. Binance Adds More Withdrawal Routes on November 3 After Security Checks

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Binance’s November 3 security-recovery notice set out a wider withdrawal restart for additional tokens and networks beginning around 04:00 UTC. Binance’s announcement is a company statement, not an independent certification that all systems are secure.

The subtle point is that a route reopening is a narrow, testable milestone. It is stronger than a vague promise of normal service, yet smaller than a comprehensive incident resolution. Customers trying to move funds should confirm the correct network at the moment they initiate a transaction, because an asset ticker alone is an incomplete withdrawal instruction.

Binance’s November 3 security-recovery notice set out a wider withdrawal restart for additional tokens and networks beginning around 04:00 UTC. The company is reopening routes progressively after its late-October hot-wallet incident rather than restoring every asset in one operation. Some supported routes run over Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, XRP Ledger and other networks, with availability determined by the exact token-and-chain combination. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

A customer withdrawal has several moving parts: the platform must hold the asset, approve the destination route, sign the transaction safely and be able to reconcile the result. A token can exist on multiple chains, so announcing a network reopening does not necessarily make every representation of that asset withdrawable. Binance’s route lists and live withdrawal interface, rather than a broad press headline, are the practical source for supported combinations.

The update matters because access to customer assets is the operational test after a security event. Replenishing balances is one question; returning funds through secure, reliable systems is another. A phased process may be frustrating to users, but it allows the operator to validate infrastructure and monitor transactions before widening access. It is also why reported recovery progress should not be confused with universal service restoration.

A crypto incident produces several separate timelines: containment, investigation, recovery and a return to reliable service. Those phases can overlap without finishing together. A traced wallet is not automatically frozen; a frozen balance is not automatically returned; and a reopened withdrawal route is not a completed security audit. Keeping those differences visible helps readers judge progress more accurately.

This development also connects to two subjects our newsroom has been following: Binance’s earlier staged withdrawal restart and Bitcoin payment infrastructure and node software context. They explain related market structure and should not be mistaken for evidence that every new proposal is already live.

Binance’s announcement is a company statement, not an independent certification that all systems are secure. It does not mean every customer, jurisdiction or network has identical withdrawal access. Users should ignore unsolicited messages claiming to fast-track withdrawals and use only the official app or website. Transaction fees, identity checks and asset-specific restrictions may still apply.

Operational controls matter most when a business is under stress. Security announcements should identify the system affected, the customers who can act, the evidence supporting any recovery number and what remains uncertain. Clear scope protects users from false reassurance and from unnecessary panic. It also provides a sensible basis for follow-up accountability.

Look for updated token-and-network lists, completed withdrawal confirmations and explanations of any routes that remain restricted. The quality of incident follow-up will also depend on technical disclosures and the effectiveness of the company’s controls after reopening. For now, the support notice is best read as a dated expansion of eligible routes, not an all-clear for the entire platform.

TL;DR: Binance said on November 2 that it had completed a zero-knowledge proof-of-reserves procedure for a snapshot taken October 31, following the exchange’s late-October security incident. Proof of reserves should not be described as a full financial audit, a guarantee against losses or evidence that all stolen assets have been returned.

In the aftermath of a major exploit, balance verification and service recovery are parallel tasks. Reserve attestations may restore visibility, while withdrawal readbacks show that the platform can operate. Neither should substitute for a full account of the breach. Reading the three separately makes it harder for one reassuring number to obscure unresolved questions.

Binance said on November 2 that it had completed a zero-knowledge proof-of-reserves procedure for a snapshot taken October 31, following the exchange’s late-October security incident. Its announcement listed ten major cryptoassets, including Bitcoin, Ether, USDT, BNB, Solana, USDC, XRP and several dollar tokens. The company said the affected asset replenishment programme had reached approximately 95% at the time of the update. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

A proof-of-reserves calculation tests whether a set of exchange-controlled assets can support the included customer balances under the method and date specified. Zero-knowledge techniques can help demonstrate a relationship without exposing every account balance. That is useful, but it does not automatically assess unrelated corporate liabilities, future cash flows, operational security or the completeness of every entity in a corporate group.

Publishing a new snapshot gives customers a concrete checkpoint rather than asking them to accept an undated reassurance. The advantage is comparability over time if disclosures remain consistent and complete. Yet a positive proof on October 31 cannot certify a November 3 withdrawal or prevent another attack. The most meaningful assessment combines reserve information with functioning services, incident disclosure and independent scrutiny.

A crypto incident produces several separate timelines: containment, investigation, recovery and a return to reliable service. Those phases can overlap without finishing together. A traced wallet is not automatically frozen; a frozen balance is not automatically returned; and a reopened withdrawal route is not a completed security audit. Keeping those differences visible helps readers judge progress more accurately.

Hyperliquid’s native token (HYPE) responded with confident growth to the historic decision of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which for the first time allowed trading of perpetual futures on individual stocks (Equity Perpetuals).

The regulatory shift de facto legitimizes a product that developed predominantly in DeFi ecosystems and opens the way for the institutional expansion of Hyperliquid’s infrastructure, which served as the trigger for the asset’s rally.

According to the CFTC release of November 3, 2026, equity perpetual contracts received the status of security futures under joint CFTC and SEC oversight, with the possibility of trading on dual-registered exchanges.

Today, equity perps can begin trading for the first time on @CFTC registered exchanges. This move reflects my commitment to ensuring that America’s markets remain the most innovative, liquid, and well-regulated in the world. Instead of being forced to turn to offshore, unregulated venues to access equity perpetual futures, Americans may now access equity perps on CFTC-regulated markets subject to robust safeguards. I appreciate the continued partnership of @SECGov and @SECPaulSAtkins as we work to further harmonize our agencies' regulatory initiatives.

The agency’s goal is to bring back into the U.S. legal field billions in volume that had been flowing to offshore crypto platforms. The instrument is being launched under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 (CFMA), which eliminates the need to pass new laws.

The regulator’s pragmatic step directly boosts Hyperliquid’s capitalization. Through its HIP-3 framework (in particular, the trade[XYZ] platform), the project already controls the largest on-chain market for perps on Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, with daily turnover in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

The new CFTC classification fully matched the structure that the Hyperliquid Policy Center advocated in official submissions to the authorities.

Now financial giant ICE (owner of the NYSE), which previously invested in trade[XYZ], gets a legal basis for creating a regulated American platform on Hyperliquid technology, while Payward (Kraken’s parent company) is accelerating the launch of a similar product through the regulated exchange Bitnomial.

Despite legalization in the U.S., Hyperliquid maintains a strict geoblock for American residents, continuing to serve the global market thanks to its key trump cards: on-chain liquidity, 24/7 trading and flexible margin conditions.

Local exchanges in the U.S. will inevitably face the limitations of traditional Wall Street sessions and strict SEC leverage limits in the early stages.

This moves Hyperliquid from the status of an offshore experiment into the role of the main technology donor of the American financial market, with the possibility of monetizing its infrastructure through fee opportunities from the trades of regulated partners.

The market instantly priced these prospects into the asset’s value. TradingView charts recorded a vertical surge in the HYPE/USD pair immediately after the release was published at 14:02 UTC: the price impulsively broke out of the $84.9-$85.30 corridor tested a local high above $87.40 and consolidated around $86.83, holding a net gain of more than 2%.

TL;DR: Tether said on November 2 that it froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT linked to the late-October Binance attack, working with investigators and industry partners. Tether’s announcement gives the company’s account of its involvement; it does not independently establish the ultimate ownership or recoverability of every frozen token.

It is tempting to present freezing power as either an unqualified feature or a fatal flaw. The more useful comparison is with the protections and limits users expect from banks and payment providers. In both worlds, legal compliance can restrict access, yet the remedy process and transparency of decisions matter just as much as the initial intervention.

Tether said on November 2 that it froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT linked to the late-October Binance attack, working with investigators and industry partners. The company said it moved quickly after receiving actionable intelligence. The claim describes issuer-enforced restrictions on specified token balances; a freeze is not the same thing as completed asset recovery or money already returned to victims. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

Centralised stablecoins can include smart-contract functions that allow the issuer to block transfers by designated addresses. This gives law-enforcement partners a tool that does not exist in the same form for native Bitcoin. But it also makes a particular promise implicit in the product: the ability to transact depends in part on an issuer retaining authority over the transfer rules.

The case illustrates a genuine trade-off. The power to immobilise suspected stolen funds may increase the chance that investigators preserve value while they work. The same central control raises questions about mistaken identification, appeals, transparency and the geographic reach of private restrictions. Stablecoins are often used because they feel like simple digital dollars, yet their governance can be as consequential as their transaction speed.

The phrase “digital dollar” can obscure important differences between products. A stablecoin holder faces an issuer and its reserve arrangements; an exchange user faces trading and custody arrangements; a merchant faces conversion and settlement partners. A good assessment follows that chain of obligations instead of assuming a one-dollar target eliminates counterparty risk.

For additional perspective, it is worth reading our existing reporting on Binance’s earlier phased withdrawal restart and the September-end Tether reserve disclosure. They explain related market structure and should not be mistaken for evidence that every new proposal is already live.

Tether’s announcement gives the company’s account of its involvement; it does not independently establish the ultimate ownership or recoverability of every frozen token. Some illicit proceeds may have moved through assets or networks outside the issuer’s control. And a publicly reported freeze total cannot be added to other recovery figures without checking whether they cover the same funds.

Stablecoin adoption depends heavily on ordinary financial services at the edges. Funding accounts, meeting identity rules, accessing banking partners and redeeming balances remain necessary even if a token transfer settles quickly. A project that solves those steps can be useful, but that usefulness cannot be established from headline issuance or a partnership announcement alone.

Watch for validated recoveries, legally authorised unfreezing or transfer procedures and clearer accounting of overlapping industry freeze figures. The longer-term issue is whether issuers can develop fast, reviewable processes that protect innocent users while meeting legitimate law-enforcement demands. A successful freeze is the start of an asset-preservation story, not necessarily its final chapter.

#5241. Aave borrowers faced up to 36% APR while a freeze blocked fresh collateral

Aave's emergency freeze left borrowers paying interest while blocking the fresh deposits that higher rates normally attract.

Borrowers in Aave's frozen reserves kept paying interest while the restrictions prevented fresh deposits, including the extra collateral they might normally supply to protect a loan. Suppliers were still able to request their money back, provided enough tokens were available, so withdrawals could make borrowing more expensive even though new borrowing was blocked in those reserves.

That left Aave with a rate mechanism whose deposit incentive couldn't work in frozen reserves. More expensive borrowing encourages people to repay and offers better returns to anyone willing to lend, but the freeze prevented that second group from putting money in. Cutting rates could give borrowers some relief, while doing nothing by itself to return the tokens suppliers wanted to withdraw.

The restrictions were introduced during the Oct. 29 Binance hot-wallet incident, and the affected reserves had reopened by Oct. 31.

LlamaRisk's recommendations to reduce borrowing rates temporarily, then restore their earlier settings, explain how protecting a lending market can leave its existing users needing different things from the same pool of money.

Someone using Aave can supply crypto as collateral and borrow another token against it, obtaining funds without selling the original holding. If you want dollars while keeping your Ethereum, for example, you can borrow a dollar-linked token such as USDC.

Those borrowed tokens come from other users who supplied them to Aave's lending contracts, the blockchain programs that handle the transactions. Suppliers earn interest while borrowers owe it. However, the same person can be both a supplier and a borrower with different assets. Supplying ETH as security for a USDC loan doesn't mean you've supplied the USDC that someone else wants to withdraw.

During the Binance hack, a wallet linked to exploiters had already supplied about $60 million of USDT and borrowed 19,762 WETH, according to LlamaRisk's account. The provider described the position as overcollateralized, meaning its collateral exceeded its debt, and said it was subject to normal liquidation. The restrictions were intended to limit further use of Aave during an external compromise.

Freezing the affected reserves stopped new supply and borrowing while repayments, withdrawals, and liquidations were still enabled. Therefore, existing debt continued to accumulate interest, but borrowers couldn't supply extra collateral into those frozen reserves.

Repayment could still reduce the debt, provided the borrower could obtain the necessary tokens. If you've borrowed USDC against ETH, repaying requires USDC, while adding more ETH would ordinarily let you support the debt without reducing it. Losing the second option narrows how you can manage the position, especially if the collateral's market price is falling at the same time.

Under Aave's liquidation rules, the health factor divides collateral value, adjusted by its liquidation threshold, by total debt. Below one, the position becomes eligible for liquidation, allowing another participant to repay debt and receive collateral plus a bonus. Interest adds to the debt side of that calculation even if the collateral price doesn't move.

However, suppliers depended on a different balance: how much of the token they wanted was actually available to withdraw. In a simplified pool with 100 USDC supplied and 90 USDC borrowed, only 10 USDC is immediately unborrowed, even if every loan has ample collateral behind it. Collateral supporting those loans doesn't turn into additional USDC just because a supplier wants to leave.

If suppliers withdraw five of those available tokens while the debt stays at 90 USDC, the pool now has 95 USDC supplied and only five available. The borrowed share has increased from 90% to about 94.7%, despite nobody taking out another loan. This is what utilization measures, and it explains how withdrawals can make a frozen market more expensive for borrowers who haven't touched their accounts.

Aave's rate formula charges more as utilization increases, with a stronger response beyond a configured threshold. Its upper section is controlled by a parameter called Slope2. Normally, higher borrowing costs encourage repayment while better supplier returns can attract fresh funds, and both can replenish the tokens available for withdrawal. During the freeze, new deposits were prohibited, leaving repayment as the available channel among those two responses.

That's why LlamaRisk recommended reducing that upper rate response. Its rationale attributed utilization of 92% to 100% in major stablecoin reserves to supplier withdrawals during the freeze, with annual borrowing rates of 10% to 36% under the settings then in place. Those were annualized rates, so a few hours at 36% didn't add 36% to someone's debt.

To put the scale in dollars, a hypothetical $10,000 loan at a constant 36% annual percentage rate would accrue roughly $9.86 in one day, versus about $2.74 at 10%, ignoring compounding and fees.

Reducing that bill also reduces the interest available to support supplier returns. Suppliers may prefer more interest, but someone trying to withdraw needs the underlying token, and Aave permits withdrawals only against available liquidity, subject to the account's collateral requirements. Even an attractive quoted yield can't pay for something outside the protocol until the supplier can retrieve the tokens.

Once fresh supply was possible again, a higher rate could once more attract deposits, giving LlamaRisk a reason to recommend restoring the earlier upper slopes on Oct. 31. Its published comparison held each reserve's utilization constant to show what the proposed settings would do, rather than recording what borrowers subsequently paid.

Borrowing APR for five Aave V3 USDC reserves at each reserve's Oct. 31, 2026, 18:05 UTC utilization. Compares temporary settings with proposed restored settings, holding utilization fixed within each reserve. These are LlamaRisk's published modeled rates, not a before-and-after time series or realized interest bills. Values retain source rounding; no interpolation.

Source: LlamaRisk, Oct. 31, 2026, Aave V3 comparison at 18:05 UTC

Core USDC was at its 94% threshold, where restoring the upper slope produced no immediate increase in the modeled rate. Base USDC was beyond its own threshold, so the same kind of intervention produced a much higher modeled cost. The reserve containing billions of dollars could show no immediate rate difference while the smaller reserve became more expensive, because each had different utilization and settings.

CryptoSlate's reopening coverage documented the continuing constraints. Permission to deposit or borrow, the collateral accepted for a loan, and the funds available for withdrawal determine different parts of what a user can do.

Getting more tokens back into a reserve also depends on what people actually do with those permissions. Fresh deposits and repayments add available tokens, while new borrowing and supplier withdrawals consume them.

Borrowers trying to preserve collateral consequently have a reason to want slower debt accrual, while suppliers trying to exit have a reason to want stronger repayment incentives.

#5240. 99% Cold Wallet Rule Mulled by South Korea Following Binance Hack

South Korean financial regulators are reportedly considering introducing much stricter cryptocurrency storage requirements for local exchanges following the massive $6.3 billion Binance hack.

According to a Nov. 3 report by South Korean news outlet News1, the country’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) is discussing raising the minimum proportion of customer cryptocurrencies that exchanges must store in cold wallets from the current 80% to approximately 99%.

The potential regulatory change comes just days after Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suffered one of the biggest security breaches in cryptocurrency history.

However, the proposed 99% threshold remains under discussion, and no official decision has been made.

Under South Korea’s existing Virtual Asset User Protection Act, cryptocurrency exchanges are required to store at least 80% of customers’ digital assets in cold wallets.

Unlike hot wallets, which are connected to the internet and used to process everyday transactions, cold wallets are kept offline, making them significantly less vulnerable to remote hacking attacks.

However, the proportion of assets stored offline varies significantly among South Korea’s leading cryptocurrency exchanges.

According to Financial Supervisory Service data cited by local media, Upbit currently has one of the highest cold wallet storage ratios in the country.

As of the end of September, the exchange held approximately 99.17% of customer assets in cold wallets.

Meanwhile, rival cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb stored approximately 94.76% of its assets offline, while Coinone’s cold wallet ratio stood at 85%.

The timing is notable because the company had separately disclosed large Bitcoin holdings at the end of October. A new acquisition can be checked against that earlier snapshot, but readers should not merge numbers from different dates without adjustment. Preferred-stock capital structure is less eye-catching than the coin count, yet it can be decisive when market conditions change.

Strategy announced on November 2 that it had acquired another 811 Bitcoin for roughly $65.5 million and repurchased approximately $208.2 million of its STRC preferred shares. The disclosure combines two very different capital-allocation decisions: increasing BTC holdings and reducing a class of outstanding preferred equity. Investors should assess both parts rather than treat the announcement as a simple Bitcoin purchase notice. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

Purchasing Bitcoin increases the company’s direct exposure to the asset. Repurchasing preferred shares changes the number of securities outstanding and can affect financing obligations, investor returns and how management uses available capital. STRC is not common equity, so its buyback has different implications from repurchasing ordinary shares; the security’s terms and price matter.

Treasury-company headlines often focus on how many coins were added, but financing costs help determine whether that strategy creates durable shareholder value. The simultaneous buyback is a useful reminder that a Bitcoin-heavy balance sheet must still be funded and managed. If new securities are issued at one point and repurchased later, the relevant comparison involves proceeds, purchase prices and future distributions.

Fund flows and corporate Bitcoin holdings share one characteristic: they are easy to count and harder to interpret. A securities wrapper reports its own creations and redemptions; a public company reports transactions inside a particular capital structure. Neither dataset captures every spot-market participant. A useful analysis establishes the reporting date, identifies what was measured and asks how much the disclosed activity represents relative to the wider market.

This development also connects to two subjects our newsroom has been following: Strategy’s earlier capital-management review and the company’s expanded Bitcoin financing framework. Those background reports help separate established facts from a new, still-developing announcement.

The dollar amounts are those disclosed by Strategy for the specified transactions. They do not, on their own, establish the company’s total current market value, future BTC acquisitions or returns to every class of shareholder. Nor should an accounting gain on Bitcoin be treated as cash generated by ordinary operations without looking at the underlying financial statements.

The critical operational issue is access to liquid Bitcoin exposure. A fund shareholder may own a listed security, while a corporate treasury holder owns shares in a company with liabilities and management decisions. Those two instruments can behave differently even when Bitcoin is the most visible asset behind both. Treating the wrapper as identical to the coin erases meaningful risks.

Next, monitor additional regulatory filings, financing terms and the ratio of Bitcoin acquisitions to securities issuance or retirement. For a business whose public narrative is built around BTC accumulation, the balance-sheet mechanics are increasingly part of the investment thesis. The quantity of Bitcoin is clear; the economic cost of obtaining and maintaining that exposure takes more work to understand.

A fresh annual report of British company VivoPower PLC, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 2, 2026, officially disclosed the parameters of the closure of its cryptocurrency strategy.

The documents recorded the creation and subsequent liquidation of a $5 million stake in the private company Ripple Labs, while also making public the price of their buyback at $300 apiece.

According to the filing, in May 2025, VivoPower announced a large-scale treasury expansion with a target investment volume of up to $100 million in XRP tokens and Ripple Labs equity. In practice, the investments turned out to be more modest: the XRP treasury allocated $5.0 million to the direct acquisition of 41,810 Ripple Labs shares in January 2026.

For institutional investors, buying stakes in the fintech giant itself was a key way to make a large bet on the ecosystem's success.

However, the experiment lasted only nine months from its announcement. As early as February, VivoPower's board of directors decided to fully wind down the crypto direction. Management recognized holding digital assets as less profitable than developing artificial intelligence infrastructure and redirected capital to the purchase of a 41.5 MW data center in Mo i Rana, Norway, for $37.7 million.

The process of liquidating this $5 million stake brought the crypto market an important price insight. In April 2026, Ripple Labs conducted a targeted buyback, taking 882 shares from VivoPower at $300 apiece. The deal brought the British company $264,600 in cash and $159,122 in net profit, giving the community a rare and hard marker of how Ripple's management itself values its business in private trades.

A direct sale of the remaining part of the stake on the open market proved impossible due to the non-public status of the securities. As a result, VivoPower entered into agreements to sell the economic rights to the shares to two South Korean partners, KWeather Co. and Lean Ventures.

As of the filing date, the Korean deals have not yet been legally completed. The remaining 40,928 shares are locked in the Korea Securities Depository (KSD) under a strict one-year lock-up restriction. Due to this freeze and the lack of market liquidity, independent appraisers lowered the book value of this stake to $4.3 million (about $106.16 per share).

The VivoPower story clearly showed the crypto industry the flip side of institutional investments: a direct purchase of stakes in Ripple Labs comes with strict lock-ups and low liquidity, where the only fast source of fiat for exiting the ecosystem is the issuer itself through a private buyback procedure.

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: BitMine Immersion Technologies reported holdings of 6,060,506 ETH as of November 1 in a November 2 filing exhibit. Cryptocurrency balance sheets are sensitive to valuation dates.

The filing’s detailed token count is valuable precisely because it can be compared with later disclosures. It also exposes a blind spot in quick “ETH treasury” comparisons: two companies with identical token balances could have very different liquidity, financing and operational risk. Staking arrangements are an essential part of that distinction.

BitMine Immersion Technologies reported holdings of 6,060,506 ETH as of November 1 in a November 2 filing exhibit. The company said 5,227,037 ETH were staked, alongside smaller Bitcoin holdings, cash and other positions. These are issuer-disclosed balances at a specified date, not independently observed live holdings or a claim about Ethereum’s total currently liquid supply. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

Staking means committing ETH to help secure Ethereum’s proof-of-stake network through validators or staking arrangements. Rewards depend on protocol conditions and operating choices, while access to staked assets can involve withdrawal queues or third-party arrangements. A substantial staked position may produce ongoing reward income, but it is not equivalent to holding the same amount in immediately transferable cash.

BitMine’s size makes its liquidity choices important. A large corporate ETH owner may hold a long-term position, but the market will still examine potential issuance, borrowing, staking income and the ability to rebalance. The issuer says its holdings represent a notable share of ETH’s supply; the comparison is a company calculation and should be tied to the supply and price assumptions used.

Ethereum has multiple sources of demand and risk: trading, staking, stablecoin settlement, application fees and long-term treasury allocation. A change in one part of that system should be tested against the others instead of promoted into a universal explanation. The market often overreacts when one publicly available metric is mistaken for the whole network economy.

For additional perspective, it is worth reading our existing reporting on BitMine’s earlier ETH accumulation and staking disclosure and our Ethereum market reporting. Those background reports help separate established facts from a new, still-developing announcement.

Cryptocurrency balance sheets are sensitive to valuation dates. A dollar figure derived from the company’s ETH price assumption can change materially without any coins moving. Staking rewards should also be separated from share-price performance and company operating costs. A large token position does not by itself tell shareholders whether their ownership is increasing or being diluted.

For investors, the right comparison is between liquidity, expected holding period and obligations. Staked ETH, ETF shares and treasury holdings may all track the same underlying asset, but their exit routes and operating constraints differ. A useful report therefore asks not simply how much ETH is involved, but how readily the exposure can be changed when conditions deteriorate.

Look for future reports distinguishing unstaked liquidity, locked or queued balances, reward income, cash uses and equity issuance. Those measures will tell investors more about treasury resilience than the headline ETH number alone. For Ethereum, the interesting network question is whether institutional-sized staking concentrations affect how observers assess operator diversity and risk.

#5233. Tesla, Amazon Deal Fresh Blow to OKX Tokenization Push

OKX has suffered another big blow to its grand aspirations of tokenizing stocks after Tesla, Amazon, and four other big names turned down plans for the tokenization of their shares on the cryptocurrency exchange’s joint venture with New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE).

Six new companies have raised objections to their shares being tokenized on the OKXICE platform.

Among the new objectors are Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX, e-commerce giant Amazon, streaming giant Netflix, semiconductor equipment maker Lam Research and fintech firm SoFi Technologies.

The new objections bring the total number of companies that have objected to the initiative to 56, further damaging OKX’s push into the realm of traditional finance.

In particular, five of the Magnificent Seven tech companies have turned down the proposal to have their stocks tokenized on the OKXICE platform. These include Tesla, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia.

What makes this rejection even more noteworthy is that the total number of targeted companies involved in this OKXICE joint venture is relatively low.

Back in early October, OKX and ICE announced their plan to offer tokenized versions of 62 major companies’ stocks.

However, 49 out of those 62 companies have formally opposed the proposal. Hence, about 79% of the initially targeted companies have rejected the plan. The other seven objections came from companies not in the initial selection.

Some of the most famous names in American finance and tech, including JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Walmart, Coca-Cola, Intel, Oracle, AMD, Nike and Costco, have also expressed their objections.

As of the Nov. 2 notice, only 13 out of the original selection had yet to raise a publicly disclosed objection.

These names include Apple, Coinbase, Robinhood, Strategy, Circle and Palantir.

However, the fact that they have not raised a formal objection doesn’t necessarily mean they approve of the tokenization plan.

It is worth noting that Nov. 3 marks the end of the 30-day objection period for the companies that received their initial notice on Oct. 4.

Nonetheless, with almost four-fifths of the initially targeted companies raising objections, OKXICE faces an uphill battle to get sufficient corporate involvement to make its tokenized stock market appealing to investors.

OKXICE has not set a definite launch date yet. It also has not disclosed the number of tokenized stocks it will offer when it starts trading.

#5231. Bitcoin Lightning fix blocks a probe linking private channels to onchain funding

LDK’s fix blocks a funding-location probe that required connections to both endpoints of an unannounced channel.

Bitcoin Optech highlighted the change on October 30. An unannounced channel stays out of the public network map, but that alone did not prevent LDK’s message-forwarding lookup from confirming its funding link.

A real short-channel ID, or SCID, works like blockchain coordinates. The Lightning specification defines it using the block height, the transaction’s position within that block and the output’s position within that transaction. Together, those identify the particular Bitcoin output funding a channel.

An attacker can derive a candidate ID from an output’s location without yet knowing whether it belongs to a channel between the suspected nodes. The documented probe supplies that missing confirmation. It requires the attacker to connect to both endpoints and construct an onion-message path through them that returns to the attacker.

Before the fix, LDK’s channel lookup could resolve a real SCID even for an unannounced channel once its funding confirmed. If the message returned successfully, the attacker could confirm that the guessed output and the channel between those nodes matched.

Requires attacker connections to both suspected endpoints and a candidate real SCID. Rejection excepts a value equal to the outbound alias. The merge does not establish release inclusion or deployed wallet coverage.

The demonstrated leak therefore joins two pieces of information: a Bitcoin funding output and the Lightning nodes using it.

LDK now refuses to resolve an unannounced channel’s real SCID for onion-message forwarding. Valid aliases remain usable as alternative identifiers, so a sender can address the channel without using its real blockchain coordinates. The change closes this lookup route while preserving forwarding that uses an allowed alias.

The change is described in the pull request. Under BOLT 4’s onion-routing rules, an onion-message SCID must correspond to an announced identifier or a local alias.

The fix’s inclusion in installed wallet versions remains unverified. Users need confirmation from their wallet provider before assuming installed software has this protection.

#5230. Kraken restricts accounts linked to suspected $133M crypto theft

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

With more than $133 million tied to alleged crypto theft carried out from an unknown entity in Europe now frozen, Kraken has issued a statement.  It said it was working with law enforcement agencies in an attempt to recover the funds.

The response was after blockchain investigator ZachXBT’s discovery of more withdrawals connected to the suspected theft. The victim’s identity and how access to the funds was obtained is not known yet.

Kraken platform said it was investigating reports that some assets subsequently moved through accounts on its platform.

Kraken also said its security systems were uncompromised, no customer accounts had been taken over, and customers faced no ongoing risk.

The alleged theft was first reported by ZachXBT on November 2, who said an EU-based organisation had been stolen from. He mentioned that around $106 million had allegedly been stolen from different exchanges on November 1.

On November 3,  he raised the estimate to above $133 Million. This was because he located an extra $27 Million of withdrawals. Some occurred with drawn funds since his publicly launched alert, he stated.

He had hinted at the victim being a large financial house in Western Europe.

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery separately traced USDC withdrawals worth $108.8 million from what it identified as wallets under Kraken, Crypto.com, and OKX.

Bitquery looked at Ethereum transactions involving some exchange wallets on November 1–2. Its narrower coverage and earlier reporting cutoff was what made its report different from ZachXBT’s.

It said about $62.98 million in stablecoins was exchanged for 27,553 ETH within about four hours.

As of November 2, around $78.3 million remained in the wallets it linked to the suspected attacker. About $30.5 million had moved beyond those tracked funds through exchanges, bridges and other services.

Crypto.com reportedly said it had acted to block the funds that were linked to the incident from moving through its platform. That its services remained operational and user funds were safe.

Reportedly, OKX also acknowledged that it was looking into the matter.

#5229. Aave Freezes New tBTC Supply and Borrowing After Mint-and-Redeem Pause

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Aave contributors said the protocol had frozen additional tBTC supply and borrowing in its Ethereum Core market after Threshold’s temporary pause of the token’s mint-and-redeem functions. It would be misleading to conclude that tBTC has lost its Bitcoin backing solely because mint and redemption were paused.

This case demonstrates why collateral quality is more complicated than an asset ticker. A wrapped token can track the price of Bitcoin under normal conditions yet carry an extra dependency on bridges, custodians and redemption operations. Lending protocols have to manage those risks separately from the volatility of the underlying coin.

Aave contributors said the protocol had frozen additional tBTC supply and borrowing in its Ethereum Core market after Threshold’s temporary pause of the token’s mint-and-redeem functions. The Aave response was activated on October 31. The restriction is specific to that asset and market; the notice did not describe a blanket freeze of unrelated Aave lending pools. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.

Wrapped Bitcoin assets represent claims or accounting mechanisms that connect Bitcoin exposure to another chain. If the mint or redemption bridge is temporarily unavailable, liquidity can change even while the token continues to trade. Lending markets react by limiting new positions that might increase risk, while allowing existing debt repayment and collateral withdrawal subject to normal account health.

An important point for borrowers is that pausing new tBTC activity does not itself change the liquidation threshold. Existing users can still face liquidation if collateral values or borrowing positions move enough to breach their health requirements. That is why a precautionary freeze and a liquidation event should not be treated as synonyms.

Decentralised lending introduces risk factors that are easy to miss if readers focus only on collateral prices. Market parameters, oracle design, token wrappers, governance powers and liquidity all affect what a user can actually do. Restrictions can reduce new exposure while leaving existing accounts sensitive to market movements. The correct interpretation starts with the exact affected pool and the functions that remain available.

This development also connects to two subjects our newsroom has been following: Aave’s first externally curated V4 lending markets and Aave’s proposed liquidation-related safeguards. They explain related market structure and should not be mistaken for evidence that every new proposal is already live.

It would be misleading to conclude that tBTC has lost its Bitcoin backing solely because mint and redemption were paused. The governance discussion describes a protective response to a specific operating condition, not a definitive finding of insolvency or fraud. The impact on an individual position depends on its collateral mix, borrowed assets and access to market liquidity.

A protocol may be automated, but its risk policy still has to be defined and maintained by people. New assets bring new dependencies; bridges and wrapped tokens add operational points of failure. Users need clear information about repayment, collateral withdrawal and liquidation conditions. Without that detail, a statement about “pausing DeFi” can be almost meaningless.

Watch Threshold’s official timeline for restoring mint and redemption, liquidity conditions for tBTC and any Aave governance proposal to amend market parameters. Users with existing positions should read the precise market notice rather than rely on headlines about a “DeFi freeze”. Clear, asset-specific communication is particularly important when markets move faster than governance procedures.

#5228. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse Breaks Silence on XRP vs. RLUSD Debate

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse addressed the ongoing debate over the potential impact of Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin on XRP’s future, asserting that both assets are complementary rather than competitive.

On Nov. 3, Brad Garlinghouse offered his view in response to a comprehensive X post from a notable member of the XRP Ledger community named Vet, who outlined the key differences between the two assets associated with Ripple.

“Well said, Vet. Complementary, not competitive,” the Ripple chief executive tweeted.

The brief statement comes amid pushback as some XRP holders are increasingly concerned that Ripple’s aggressive foray into the stablecoin market may negatively impact demand for XRP in the future.

As part of his viral post, Vet explained that the key difference between the two assets revolves around the purposes they serve on the XRP Ledger.

“RLUSD is optional. XRP isn’t,” the commentator explained.

As the XRP Ledger’s native currency, XRP is essential for the core functions of the network. First, every account must have an XRP reserve. Second, transaction fees are paid in XRP.

RLUSD, on the other hand, is a dollar-denominated stablecoin issued by Ripple's regulated stablecoin business. The key difference is that, unlike XRP, the value of RLUSD is supposed to remain stable at roughly $1.

Another key difference lies in control over the assets.

Ripple has the ability to freeze RLUSD under certain conditions, for example, to meet legal obligations. There is no central entity that can freeze XRP, the native cryptocurrency, on the ledger.

According to Vet, another key advantage of XRP is its privileged status on the XRP Ledger's DEX.

The XRP Ledger has an automatic bridging function. In this way, if it makes sense to trade between currencies through XRP for a better exchange rate, trades can be automatically routed through XRP.

This is why XRP is so valuable for liquidity providers and market makers as an intermediary asset.

On the other hand, RLUSD would be much more suitable in cases where price stability is important, for example, for payroll, invoicing, corporate payments, etc.

At the same time, some XRP investors are worried that one day RLUSD may effectively replace XRP for some payment use cases.

The crucial question is this: If you can send a dollar-denominated stablecoin directly, why would you need to use an intermediary like XRP?

It’s also worth noting that RLUSD isn’t exclusive to the XRP Ledger. In fact, RLUSD also works on Ethereum and other supported blockchains. So increasing demand for RLUSD doesn’t necessarily lead to more use of the XRP Ledger.

And even if we’re seeing more RLUSD transactions on the XRP Ledger, this doesn’t automatically mean that increased demand for XRP to pay transaction fees necessarily guarantees a significant price surge for the cryptocurrency.

It’s not the first time Garlinghouse has been forced to comment on Ripple's changing priorities.

During Ripple’s Swell 2026 conference in New York on Oct. 28, Ripple’s CEO directly addressed rumors that Ripple is becoming increasingly focused on RLUSD rather than XRP.

“We will never give up on XRP,” Garlinghouse said.

#5227. Bitcoin and Treasury yields fall together in rare divergence as $80,000 recovery fails

Bitcoin dropped 8.25% while real yields declined 16 basis points, raising questions about why a historically supportive macroeconomic shift has offered little relief.

Bitcoin is struggling to recover despite falling US Treasury yields, as technology-stock weakness and persistent ETF withdrawals weigh on demand.

Between Oct. 21 and Oct. 30, the world's largest cryptocurrency declined 8.25%, falling from approximately $84,134 to $77,191, according to CryptoSlate's data.

Over the same period, the Federal Reserve's data shows that yields on 10-year inflation-protected US Treasuries fell from 2.76% to 2.60%, down 16 basis points. The Nasdaq-100 also lost 4.82%, reflecting mounting pressure on technology stocks.

The divergence is notable because lower real Treasury yields typically reduce the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. However, selling pressure across crypto and parts of the equity market has overwhelmed that potential support.

The weakness continued into November. On Nov. 2, the Nasdaq-100 declined another 1.39%, while Bitcoin's daily Coinbase price observation fell 1.34% to approximately $77,062 from the previous day.

Bitcoin was trading near $76,861 early Tuesday, leaving it below the psychologically important $80,000 level.

Bitfinex attributed the weakness to declining technology shares and subdued spot-market demand, arguing that those pressures were overwhelming the potential support from falling real Treasury yields.

The selling pressure was compounded by Binance's Oct. 29 security breach, which crypto trading firm Wintermute identified as the dominant crypto-specific shock behind last week's downturn.

The incident struck an already fragile market, triggering about $1.5 billion in crypto liquidations, with long positions accounting for approximately 85% of the total.

Wintermute said traders had attempted to buy the decline primarily through leveraged perpetual futures rather than sustained spot purchases. As prices continued falling, those positions faced further liquidation, deepening the downturn.

The firm warned that there was little evidence of fresh capital entering the market to support a durable recovery.

The weakness has also extended to US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which recorded $398.6 million in net outflows on Nov. 2, according to Farside Investors.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for $405.3 million in withdrawals, partially offset by $6.7 million in inflows into Fidelity's FBTC.

That followed $643.2 million in ETF outflows on Oct. 30, bringing total net withdrawals across the two trading sessions to approximately $1.04 billion.

The sustained redemptions have added to concerns about Bitcoin's ability to recover, particularly as Wintermute's analysis suggests that recent buying has been concentrated in leveraged derivatives rather than supported by substantial new spot-market capital.

#5224. Hong Kong bank pilot opens 24/7 cash settlement for tokenized fund deals

Participating institutions can settle tokenized deposit transactions in central bank money beyond conventional hours, supporting treasury and fund activity.

Hong Kong's tokenization pilot now lets participating banks settle tokenized deposit transactions around the clock in central bank money, extending the cash settlement behind corporate treasury and tokenized-fund activity beyond conventional operating hours.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced the upgrade on Nov. 2. EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, now has 12 participating banks and 20 industry pioneers.

The customer deposits and the settlement money have different roles. Participating firms use tokenized deposits supplied by commercial banks; tokenized central bank money settles the transactions between banks. The upgrade extends the hours available for that interbank cash settlement.

Participating industry pioneers have already used bank-provided tokenized deposits for corporate treasury management and tokenized money market fund transactions. HKMA names Ant International, BlackRock and China Asset Management (Hong Kong) among the firms involved.

Banks providing tokenized deposits for the cited activity include Bank of China (Hong Kong), China Construction Bank (Asia), ICBC (Asia), Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong) and HSBC. These are examples given by HKMA, rather than the full roster of 12 participating banks.

For a corporate treasury using the pilot, the practical change is that its participating bank can settle the relevant transactions outside conventional operating hours. Tokenized-fund users gain extended cash-settlement availability where their banks and platforms support the activity.

Securities and Futures Commission Chief Executive Julia Leung said the capability supports round-the-clock corporate treasury transactions and secondary trading of tokenized funds on licensed platforms. Availability for an individual fund still depends on the bank and platform arrangements; continuous interbank settlement does not establish continuous trading for every fund.

#5219. North Korea denies role in $6 billion Binance hack after FBI accusation

Reuters, citing KCNA, reported the denial after the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing more than $6 billion from Binance.

Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed US claims linking the country to the Binance hack as “absurd rhetoric,” Reuters reported on Nov. 2, citing the Korean Central News Agency, or KCNA. The denial disputes the US government's attribution of the theft of more than $6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange.

The FBI had blamed North Korea's TraderTraitor operation in an Oct. 31 alert, placing the theft on or about Oct. 29. TraderTraitor is the bureau's name for the specific North Korean cyber activity it identified in the attack.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs estimated that approximately $6 billion left Binance wallets across ten blockchains, with most of the funds moving in about 20 minutes beginning at 20:05 UTC on Oct. 29. The firm's initial figures reflected observations through 00:30 UTC on Oct. 30.

TRM attributed the Binance hack to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing on-chain and off-chain intelligence.

The firm also assessed that valid signed transfers across different blockchains pointed to a compromise of Binance's hot-wallet signing infrastructure. That would place the breach in the systems used to authorize outgoing wallet transactions. The explanation remains TRM's assessment of how the transfers were enabled. #5213. Crypto spent $55 million defending a senator who already backed CLARITY

One of crypto's most expensive election bets is playing out in Ohio, where winning could leave the industry's biggest problem in Washington untouched.

Defend American Jobs, a crypto-backed political group, spent more than $55 million supporting Republican Jon Husted and opposing Sherrod Brown in Ohio between Sept. 21 and Oct. 26, according to Americans for Financial Reform. Husted had already voted to advance the CLARITY Act.

Americans vote today, Nov. 3, in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. Republicans currently control both chambers.

Congress has to agree on crypto legislation, which means winning over enough lawmakers in both parties to get it passed.

The midterms will shape committee leadership, hearings and the path to a vote. Presidents appoint regulators and set enforcement priorities, but a later administration can change those policies.

Crypto-backed groups have poured money into congressional races, often backing candidates based on their crypto positions rather than their party.

Fairshake and its affiliated groups have become some of the biggest spenders in American politics, with a Reuters analysis estimating that crypto groups had spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 races by late October.

Ohio has become a major focus of that strategy.

Husted already voted in September to advance the CLARITY Act, a major proposal intended to establish clearer federal rules for crypto. The bill failed to clear a 60-vote Senate hurdle, leaving its supporters short of the backing needed to move forward. Brown, meanwhile, wasn't even in the Senate when that happened, having lost his previous seat in 2024 before launching a comeback campaign against Husted for Ohio's other Senate seat.

Keeping Husted in Washington would protect a vote the industry already has, while defeating Brown would prevent a prominent crypto critic from returning to Congress. Both outcomes would be politically valuable, especially with Senate control potentially at stake, but neither will resolve the disagreements that stopped the legislation in September.

That's because lawmakers are still fighting over stablecoin rewards, banking risks and the protections customers should receive when crypto companies handle their money, and the industry's expensive election campaign can't settle those disputes on its own.

Republicans currently hold 53 seats, so even a united Republican caucus would need support from outside the party to reach the 60-vote threshold used in September.

Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, and Jerry Moran all voted against moving ahead. Thom Tillis recorded a no as well, but did so to preserve the option of asking the Senate to reconsider, a procedural step that would allow another attempt rather than an expression of opposition to the bill itself.

Collins wanted further study of whether community banks and credit unions could lose deposits used to support “loans for mortgages, small businesses, and other family needs.” The dispute centers partly on stablecoin rewards. Crypto platforms offer rewards to customers who keep stablecoins in an account, giving those customers another reason to leave their money there, so banks see those offers as competition for money that might otherwise sit in a deposit account. Banking groups argue that losing those deposits could make it harder to fund lending, and they have pushed lawmakers to restrict rewards that work like interest.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The September proposal would restrict payments by third parties, such as exchanges, when those payments function like interest on bank deposits. It would still allow rewards tied to transactions or activity, which draws a distinction between paying someone to leave a balance untouched and rewarding them for actually using it.

Banking associations argue that the proposed distinction leaves ways to keep paying what is effectively interest, even when the payment is described or structured differently.

Under the September draft, Treasury could impose further restrictions if stablecoin yield caused substantial harm to community-bank deposits within 18 months of enactment. The sponsors presented that provision as protection for smaller banks and the businesses that rely on them.

Banking groups objected that waiting until significant damage had occurred would make the protection come too late. Their response called for tighter restrictions in the legislation itself, rather than relying on regulators to act after deposits had already moved.

Nevada Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto raised a different set of objections, saying the September version left unresolved problems involving illicit finance, prediction markets, and ethics. She supported the separate GENIUS stablecoin legislation, but said this proposal didn't do enough to help law enforcement address crypto crime or resolve concerns about political conflicts.

The sponsors said they incorporated 126 substantive changes requested by Democrats and revised the restrictions governing public officials’ crypto interests. Cortez Masto’s response was that important problems remained and that Republican Senate leaders had ended negotiations before they were resolved.

Those objections would still need answers after a Husted victory, unless the sponsors could find enough support elsewhere.

Even after an agreement in the Senate, the House would have to approve the same legislative text before it could go to the president. Democrats could ask for different terms from those accepted by the current chamber if they won a House majority, including in a scenario where Republicans held the Senate.

Congress can also act after the election and before its current term ends on Jan. 3, 2027. That period gives lawmakers another opportunity to negotiate.

Bills that have not become law by the end of a Congress don't carry over automatically. The legislation would need to be introduced again and work through the process, leaving the newly elected House and Senate to decide which parts of the September proposal they were willing to keep.
