#5209. The Women’s Sports Leagues to Watch This Fall and Winter, from NWSL to Unrivaled

Everyone say: “Thank you, women’s sports.”

Do you feel that chill in the air? Feels like time to stay home in a cozy sweatshirt and watch some women’s sports. Luckily, there are quite a few leagues to tune into right now, keeping us well fed through the winter.

Whether you’re a diehard fan of a team already or looking for something new to watch, these are the leagues we’re most excited about right now.

The National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) season started back in March, but if you haven’t tuned in yet, now is the time. Playoffs start November 6, with New York/New Jersey Gotham FC, San Diego Wave, and Washington Spirit already having clinched a spot.

If you even slightly enjoyed watching the U.S. Men’s National Team in the World Cup this summer, you’ll love the NWSL. The teams are made up of the epic women who play on our national team, like Trinity Rodman, Rose Lavelle, and Mallory Swanson.

Even more women’s soccer: Ahead of the FIFA Women’s World Cup next summer, the U.S. Women’s National team is also playing a series of international games in the coming months, including a match against El Salvador on November 27.

How to watch: Friday matches air on Prime Video, Saturday matches air on ION, Paramount+, and ESPN, and Sunday matchups stream for free on the Victory+ platform. You can also watch all games on NWSL+.

It’s been 200 days since the UCLA Bruins beat the University of South Carolina Gamecocks in the national championship game last year, but who’s counting? College basketball finally returns on November 1 and will run through April, with teams like the University of South Carolina, University of Connecticut, and the University of Southern California starting the season in top-ranked positions.

Players to watch: It’s a little early to start talking national player of the year, but two women have already earned that spot in previous seasons (and are heavily favored to do so again). Sarah Strong of UConn won multiple awards to round out 2026, while JuJu Watkins of University of Southern California was national player of the year in 2025. Watkins is returning after missing an entire season due to a knee injury. Other early favorites include Hannah Hidalgo at Notre Dame and Mikayla Blakes at Vanderbilt.

How to watch: NCAA basketball games air across channels including ABC, Fox, CBS, ESPN, and you can watch either with cable or streaming apps like YouTube TV, Sling, Fubo, and Hulu + Live TV.

Speaking of basketball, Unrivaled is back—and bigger than ever—in January. The season starts on the 8th with a double-header game in Boston. Then, Unrivaled hits the road and will make stops across the country in New York City, Minneapolis, Los Angeles, Detroit, San Francisco, Houston, Philadelphia, and back to its home in Miami. As someone who had the pleasure of going to an Unrivaled game in person, let me tell you: If it’s coming to your city, go! (But, watching on TV is good too.)

How it’s different from the WNBA: Unrivaled has all the best WNBA players (like Napheesa Collier, Paige Bueckers, and Breanna Stewart), but the game setup is different. Games are 3-on-3 and faster-paced. Plus, the league is setting a new standard for women’s basketball: Players have equity in the league and don’t have to play abroad during their off seasons anymore.

How to watch: Unrivaled games air on HBO Max, Tru TV, and TNT.

League One Volleyball (LOVB, pronounced “love”) is about to begin its second season, increasing the number of teams from six to 10. The “First Serve” match is set to air on December 16, in San Antonio, Texas, when the reigning champions LOVB Austin will take on LOVB Nebraska.

Something cool about the league: LOVB invests in athletes of all ages, connecting youth and junior clubs all the way up to the pros and investing in their development.

How to watch: You can watch all games on YouTube, as well as stream them on demand on USA, ESPN+, and Victory+.

#5207. Binance says thinly traded tokens are delaying full replacement of stolen assets

Binance attributes its last reported 5% replenishment gap to less-liquid assets, while its November 3 withdrawal plan reopens routes progressively.

Binance said in its Nov. 2 recovery update that less-liquid tokens were slowing the replacement of stolen assets. It put the outstanding replenishment at approximately 5% of the impacted amount, while a separate withdrawal phase was scheduled for Nov. 3.

The new phase was scheduled to begin at 04:00 UTC. In Binance's Nov. 3 update, the exchange said availability would expand progressively as security and readiness checks were completed for individual assets and networks.

Together, the disclosures explain why a commitment to cover stolen funds can coexist with unfinished recovery. Funding the purchases, obtaining the specific tokens and restoring the routes through which customers withdraw them are separate tasks.

The replenishment percentage, dated reserve proof and asset-network reopening answer different questions.

Binance said proof for ten tokens at the October 31 snapshot was complete on November 2. This concerns backing at that snapshot.

The November 3 plan reopens asset-network pairs progressively after security checks. These examples do not establish current availability.

A replenishment percentage does not establish that a particular withdrawal route is available.

Binance's statements are attributed reporting. The denominator's valuation basis is unspecified. No live route status or unreplenished token identity is established; the October 31 proof concerns ten named tokens.

Source-bound comparison of Binance's disclosures. The approximate 95/5 bar represents the stated shares of the impacted amount, not token counts, dollars or withdrawal routes. Named pairs are examples from the planned November 3 table.

Binance's statements are attributed reporting. The denominator's valuation basis is unspecified. No live route status or unreplenished token identity is established; the October 31 proof concerns ten named tokens.

Binance reported approximately 95% replenishment of the impacted amount in its Nov. 1 recovery update. It repeated that figure on Nov. 2, attributing the outstanding portion to tokens outside the ten assets it said were fully backed: BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD and ZEC.

The exchange said the remaining assets were less liquid and took longer to source in the required quantities. It described continued purchases through market and over-the-counter channels, alongside work with industry partners to finish the acquisitions.

In its Oct. 31 update, Binance identified corporate treasury, a planned partial deployment of its Secure Asset Fund for Users and a portion of its futures insurance resources as recovery funding sources.

The percentage also has a narrower meaning than a general recovery score. Binance describes the denominator as the impacted amount. It does not specify the valuation basis in those disclosures, so the remaining 5% cannot safely be converted into a dollar shortfall. Nor does 95% describe the proportion of tokens or withdrawal routes restored.

Binance's Nov. 2 update said the zero-knowledge proof for its Oct. 31, 00:00 UTC reserve snapshot was complete. It said holders of the ten named tokens could independently verify that their balances were backed at least one-for-one.

The proof concerns a defined set of assets at a dated snapshot. Backing at that snapshot does not establish present availability of every withdrawal route.

The latest withdrawal table illustrates why the network matters alongside the token. It includes RLUSD on Ethereum and XRP, and USDC on Sui, among routes planned for progressive reopening. Those entries identify the scope of the rollout, not which tokens remain unreplenished or whether each route is currently operational.

Binance said it was prioritizing tokens according to demand over the preceding week and restoring each network-asset pair after security checks.

For holders, the immediate check is the chosen asset and network. Binance directed users to its withdrawal page or network-status page to confirm availability, and warned that rollout traffic could cause temporary delays or longer processing times.

A separate transparency milestone is still ahead. Binance said it planned a Nov. 4 reserve snapshot covering more tokens, followed by proof generation estimated to take approximately 40 to 50 hours.

Binance reiterated that it would bear the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass losses on to users.

#5204. “My Runs Are Soft, Smooth, and, Once Again, Satisfying”

After three runs in the On Cloudsurfer 3, this writer finds her groove again.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: Until recently, I’d been dreading my runs. All the joy in them was gone. They felt more like a chore than an escape. They were just…hard. Every time out, my body felt heavy, my mind wandered, and staying in bed seemed so much more appealing. I needed to find my spark again: the glide, the levity, the freedom.

That’s why I decided to try On’s Cloudsurfer 3 for a few days. I was ready for a major change, something that would help me enjoy my runs again, and maybe this was it. After decades of logging miles, I wasn’t ready to accept that running wasn’t working for me anymore, mentally or physically. Luckily, after three of the softest running experiences I’ve ever had, I know I have still have many miles left in me.

Here’s my day-by-day account of testing the Cloudsurfer 3 across New York City parks, stairs, and hills:

I’ve been resting for a couple of days and my plan is to do a couple of easy miles. Unlike my other shoes, the Cloudsurfer 3 is cushioned—hyper-cushioned compared to anything that I have run in before. After lacing them up, I like how the upper mesh forms around my feet and makes them feel tucked in.

Then, I stand. Instantly I feel taller, which throws me off. I figure the extra height will translate into a soft ride, since that’s the whole point of the Surreal™ superfoam in the midsole and the geometry of the outsole. I know I’ll get used to it.

Once I’m outside, the moment of truth comes with my first propulsion. Immediately, everything seems lighter, smoother, softer. The extra height seems to be worth it. The levity and the spring from when I first started running are back; my gait is smoother than it’s been in a while, and I keep going. My plan to keep this run short gets smoked. The final tally is 5.25 practically effortless miles. When I return home, my legs don’t feel heavy and my post-workout yoga isn’t met with the normal “oohs” and “eeks.”

Last night, I dreamt about running. I can’t remember the last time that happened. My body feels good. No aches and pains like I usually have after my first run of the week. There might be something to a cushioned shoe after all. I decide to tackle some stairs and hills with a short out-and-back route to Central Park’s Bethesda Fountain stairs.

Running the steps, my toe strikes feel bouncy on the down phases and I’m able to get my knees up higher on the up. Both my heart rate and RPE rating—an 8 or 9 out of 10—tell me this is a tough workout. I climb the hill back home in a run-walk to recover, and this is when the rolling motion of the shoe feels more pronounced to me. The hill seems easier than in the past, and my heart rate recovers sooner. So I decide while exiting the park that I’m going to do streetlight intervals, alternating running and sprinting from one light to the next.

I dreamt about running again. Specifically, running Harlem Hill in the park. For those who aren’t familiar, this hill is a bear. Even though it’s only 0.3 miles, the incline can reach close to 8 percent at the top and averages around 4.5 percent. It’s brutal, and I haven’t run this hill since a half-marathon I did over a year ago, but I’m game to tackle it when I wake up. Yesterday’s runs piqued my curiosity about the Cloudsurfer 3’s performance on a more substantial incline.

Navigating the downhill switchbacks to get to the hill’s base is controlled and fast. I don’t feel like I’m pounding or lumbering down. Each step rolls from heel to toe, supported at every touchpoint. It’s a soft, smooth ride. But the real test of the day is still to come.

As I head up the hill, the roll continues to help propel me forward. The effort is greater than the day before (but so is the incline). There’s less pain than in previous passes of this run. When I get to the top I’m still winded, but my legs and glutes aren’t nearly as tired as I remember. I finish the second half of my run easily. When I get home, my overall pace says it all: 45 seconds faster per mile compared to day 1.

Thanks to Cloudsurfer 3, I found my running groove again.

Carey Rossi is the Senior News Editor for Prevention and Prevention.com. You can follow her @CareyRossi.

#5202. Bitcoin investors could pay the price as the Federal Reserve tightens bank lending rules

The Fed's Nov. 2 survey shows tougher approvals alongside stronger nonbank demand, with no evidence of forced Bitcoin sales.

Banks tightened loan approval standards for nonbank financial firms while reporting stronger demand from business lenders and private-equity funds, according to the Federal Reserve's Nov. 2 lending survey.

That combination points to a financing constraint that could limit investors' appetite for Bitcoin beyond changes in the Fed's policy rate.

For business lenders, classified as business credit intermediaries in the survey, 12 of 50 responding domestic banks tightened standards, one eased, and 37 left them unchanged. The response table shows 24% tightening versus 2% easing, for a net tightening of 22%.

The October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey covers the preceding three months, generally the third quarter. Responses were due Oct. 5, well before the late-October spread widening.

Domestic banks reported net tightening across all five nonbank borrower categories surveyed. They most often cited a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook and deterioration in borrowers' financial strength.

At the same time, banks reported stronger demand from business credit intermediaries and private-equity funds in a question measuring funds actually disbursed.

A minority of banks tightened business-lender standards, producing a 22-point net balance. The survey and market indicators describe different periods.

Approval tightening is real, but neither its bank-share measure nor these mismatched dates establishes Bitcoin selling.

Approval standards determine access to credit, so financing can become harder to obtain without a new policy-rate increase. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28, a separate decision from the earlier lending conditions captured by the survey.

If financing becomes harder to secure while liquidity needs rise, investors may have less capacity or willingness to hold risky assets. A 2023 IMF working paper found that US monetary tightening historically reduced a common crypto-price factor through that channel.

The ICE BofA US high-yield option-adjusted spread rose from 3.14% on Oct. 28 to 3.44% on Oct. 30, a widening of 30 basis points.

The Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index was -0.487 for the week ending Oct. 23, indicating conditions looser than average.

A stronger signal of spillover would be continued widening in credit premiums alongside weakening Bitcoin demand, while narrowing spreads and resilient demand would weaken that case. For now, the survey shows a financing constraint worth watching.

#5197. Binance relied on AI to fight fraud before hackers exploited internal tool in $6 billion theft

Attackers exploited an internal AI system to reach wallet engineers, prompting the exchange to seek security partnerships with leading AI companies.

Hackers exploited Binance's internal artificial intelligence tools to compromise engineers before stealing $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency, the exchange disclosed.

In its Nov. 3 security report, Binance said attackers used a compromised employee computer and an internal AI tool on Oct. 20 to take control of two engineers responsible for its wallet infrastructure.

The attackers subsequently obtained access to a container deployment permission token, which helped them penetrate the exchange's wallet-signing operations on Oct. 29 and initiate unauthorized transactions across several blockchain networks.

The disclosure puts AI at the center of one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record, adding to concerns about how increasingly connected AI systems can introduce new vulnerabilities into corporate infrastructure.

Binance's investigation does not establish that an AI model autonomously planned or executed the theft. Rather, the attackers exploited an internal AI tool as part of a broader campaign involving stolen credentials, compromised developer software, and social engineering.

In June, a Binance engineer downloaded a tampered software installer while attempting to install a popular AI coding tool. Binance detected the suspicious activity, replaced the device and rotated associated credentials, although information about the employee and colleagues had already been exposed.

In September, another engineer fell victim to a fake recruitment operation involving staged job interviews and a malicious coding assignment. The malware compromised the employee's computer and gave the attackers access, which they later used to move deeper into Binance's systems.

The FBI has attributed the broader attack to North Korea, whose hacking operations have increasingly targeted software developers and cryptocurrency businesses.

The Binance incident follows months of warnings from cybersecurity researchers that artificial intelligence is expanding both hackers' capabilities and the systems available for exploitation.

In February, Google's Mandiant reported that North Korean hackers targeting the cryptocurrency industry had incorporated AI-assisted techniques into their operations.

The researchers documented an intrusion involving a fake video conference, malicious software, and a suspected AI-generated video impersonating a corporate executive. They could not independently confirm the deepfake in that particular incident but identified the group's use of AI tools for reconnaissance and social engineering.

By September, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported that attackers were moving beyond using AI to generate malicious content toward automated operations that could execute multiple stages of an intrusion.

In one case, hackers compromised a cloud resource and organized an AI-assisted mass credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours. Google also identified attackers attempting to manipulate AI coding assistants and security scanners during software supply-chain compromises.

The findings closely resemble one aspect of the Binance breach: developers and the AI-powered tools they depend on are becoming targets attackers use to reach sensitive systems.

Separately, AI developer Anthropic disclosed in September that criminals and suspected state-sponsored operators had used its Claude models to conduct reconnaissance, develop exploitation tools, and automate data theft.

Some operations involved AI agents carrying out multiple stages of an attack with limited human supervision, reducing the technical expertise and manpower traditionally required.

The exchange is now seeking support from the same industry whose technologies were featured in the attack.

Binance said it is working to establish a security research fund and develop targeted initiatives with leading AI companies, blockchain industry participants and cybersecurity firms.

The proposed collaboration will focus on strengthening AI security in blockchain environments, although the exchange has not disclosed the fund's proposed size, participating companies or launch date.

It also plans to expand spending on AI-enabled threat detection, endpoint protection, developer-environment security and behavioral anomaly monitoring.

The exchange said it has already rebuilt the affected internal AI tool and wallet infrastructure, replaced compromised employee devices and strengthened access controls.

Binance has also commissioned an independent cybersecurity review to validate its investigation and identify additional safeguards.

The company said approximately $2.85 billion of the $6.34 billion in affected digital assets has been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of impacted token assets had been replenished as of Oct. 31.

The independent review has yet to establish the full extent of the weaknesses that allowed attackers to exploit the exchange's internal AI environment. Its findings will inform the security changes Binance plans to implement as it develops the proposed industry fund.

#5196. These Are The 7 Best Fruits to Lower Blood Pressure, According to Experts

Meet the top picks and what experts have to say about each one.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

High blood pressure can creep up on you, leading to symptoms like chest pain, headaches, and dizziness. And since the condition is linked to more serious health complications like heart attack and stroke, it’s important to stay on top of your numbers.

Blood pressure management is complex, and usually involves making a slew of lifestyle changes, including adjusting your exercise routine, tweaking your diet, and even taking medication. But when it comes to those dietary adjustments, consuming fewer packaged and ultra-processed foods and “replacing them with whole foods and antioxidant-rich foods like fruits can be helpful,” says Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers.

Meet the experts: Scott Keatley, RD, is co-owner of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy. Jessica Cording, RD, is the author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Keri Gans, RDN, is a dietitian and host of The Keri Report podcast.

There's some research to back up these claims too: A 2022 study in the Journal of Clinical Hypertension monitored their blood pressure at home in over 2,200 participants ages 50 to 65. They self-reported how often they ate bananas, apples, pears, and citrus fruit (response options were: not every week, once or twice a week, three to four times per week, and at least five times per week), and those who ate those fruits more frequently had significantly lower systolic home blood pressure.

Ahead, dietitians break down the best fruits that may help lower your blood pressure to regularly add to your plate.

The big draw with bananas is their potassium content; one medium-sized banana delivers about 375 milligrams of potassium, per the USDA, which helps you meet your daily goal of 2,600 milligrams of the nutrient, according to the NIH.

Why does this matter? Potassium “balances sodium in the body and relaxes blood vessel walls, directly lowering [blood] pressure,” explains Scott Keatley, RD, co-owner of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy. Having some sodium in the body is important, but too much will cause your body to hold onto water, according to Harvard Health. When that happens, the amount of fluid in your blood vessels increases and raises blood pressure along with it.

Blueberries contain anthocyanins, which are plant compounds that improve blood vessel flexibility and support nitric oxide production, says Keri Gans, RDN, a dietitian and host of The Keri Report podcast. Nitric oxide helps relax the smooth muscles in the blood vessels, helping them widen so blood can flow more freely, decreasing blood pressure, she explains.

This green fruit is loaded with vitamin C—59 milligrams, to be exact. (That's over half the daily recommended goal for women, which is 75 milligrams, per Mayo Clinic.) Vitamin C “enhances nitric oxide availability," Keatley says. Again, nitric oxide helps to relax the smooth muscles in your blood vessels, lowering blood pressure along with it. It also helps to relax the blood vessels, making it easier for blood to flow through and lowering blood pressure as a result.

Like kiwi, grapefruit is rich in vitamin C, as one half of a grapefruit has 39 milligrams of the nutrient, per the USDA. “Compounds [like vitamin C and potassium] in grapefruit can improve the elasticity of blood vessels and reduce oxidative stress, which helps the circulatory system function more efficiently and lowers blood pressure,” Keatley says.

Grapes are loaded with polyphenols, which are naturally-occurring chemical compounds found in plants, Cording explains. These support the elasticity of your blood vessels and reduce oxidative stress in the body, lowering the risk of inflammation—which is also a risk factor for high blood pressure, Gans adds.

Watermelon contains an amino acid called L- citrulline. It boosts the production of nitric acid in your body, helping to widen those blood vessels and lower your blood pressure, Keatley says.

Like bananas, avocados pack a potassium punch—576 milligrams is in 100 grams, or 3/4 of a cup, per the USDA—to help with blood pressure management, Keatley says. They may also help with weight management thanks to the fact the contain healthy fats that will keep you full and satiated—and that can indirectly help to reduce blood pressure, he says.

Remember: High blood pressure is complex, and consuming more fruit alone is unlikely to make it to drop. However, eating more nutritiously can support your other efforts to bring it down. If you have high blood pressure, it’s important to work closely with your healthcare provider to come up with a comprehensive plan to help turn things around.

#5192. North Korean hackers launder $242 million of Binance loot via Tron as FBI presses THORChain: analyst

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Relay and THORChain moved the largest shares of the loot off Tron, while Symbiosis and Chainflip said their screening had flaws. THORChain’s official front end has blocked the FBI-listed addresses.

North Korean hackers have laundered about $242 million of the funds stolen from Binance on the Tron blockchain in two days, onchain analyst and Security Alliance (SEAL) contributor SomaXBT said on X on Sunday, as the FBI presses THORChain and other services to block the transactions.

The attackers took about $628 million from Binance on Tron and had roughly $249 million left to move after Tether froze 378.7 million USDT, SomaXBT said in his thread. Most of the $242 million, about $194 million, left Tron through bridges and swap services. Another $26 million stayed on the network, while about $22 million went to fees, slippage and price moves, according to the analyst.

The funds moved through a variety of crypto bridges: Relay handled $48 million of the outflows, THORChain $44 million, Chainflip $32.1 million and Symbiosis $16 million, together about $140 million, SomaXBT said. Bitget Wallet handled another $41.7 million, but where that money ended up is still unresolved, the analyst said.

Binance lost about $6.3 billion on Thursday in the largest crypto hack on record. The FBI attributed the theft to the TraderTraitor group on Saturday in an alert issued with the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation.

The FBI said the hackers were converting stolen assets "primarily into Ethereum" and expects the funds to be further laundered through DeFi protocols and instant swap services. It urged THORChain's THORNode operators, alongside RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services and other providers, to block transactions tied to the theft. The agency also published a list of 608 Ethereum addresses, 19 bitcoin addresses and one Solana address, but no Tron addresses, that it said were linked to the attack.

A 2022 joint advisory from the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Treasury Department describes TraderTraitor as a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group, active since at least 2020, that steals and launders crypto "to support the North Korean regime." The advisory says the cybersecurity industry tracks the group under various designations, including Lazarus Group, APT38 and BlueNoroff.

The FBI also blamed TraderTraitor for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025. The agency's recent alert did not disclose the evidence that led it to its attribution, though blockchain analysis firms Chainalysis, Elliptic and TRM Labs had already linked the theft to North Korea through onchain ties to earlier North Korean hacks.

THORChain technical co-founder Chad Barraford wrote on X on Saturday evening that "THORNode operators have zero information that isn't already public and readily available in real time." He added, "No subpoenas required, a best case scenario for investigations," but his posts since the hack have not said whether node operators would block the listed addresses.

Earlier on Saturday, an Ethereum reorg caused THORChain to double-refund a 10 ETH deposit, which triggered an emergency pause, Chainalysis said. The pause, somewhat ironically, stopped all users, including the hackers, from swapping through most of THORChain's bridges, according to the firm.

THORChain trading remained halted on 10 of its 13 connected chains, including Tron, Ethereum and Bitcoin, as of 1:20 p.m. ET Sunday, according to THORChain node data. Trading from Tron has been halted since around midday Saturday.

In a message to The Block on Sunday, Barraford said he does not talk to node operators much and had not seen any discussion of the FBI’s request. "I assume they will be consistent and resume trading as normal," he said, adding that "the official thorchain centralized frontend has blocked the addresses requested by the FBI."

The attackers have sent 185.1 million TRX and 3.83 million USDT into THORChain in 2,697 deposits, SomaXBT said. THORChain has paid out 17,019 ETH to 170 addresses and 53.25 BTC to 20 addresses.

The attackers lost about 12% to fees and slippage, and front-end interfaces earned about 145,800 RUNE, roughly $95,000, in affiliate fees. North Korea's Lazarus Group also used THORChain to move much of the ether stolen from Bybit's $1.5 billion hack onto bitcoin in February 2025.

Relay received 37.64 million USDT and 39.28 million TRX in 735 deposits, SomaXBT said, adding that the protocol "barely featured" in laundering from past TraderTraitor hacks. Onchain analyst Specter said on Saturday that the hackers bridged $38 million through Relay in seven hours, despite Relay's statement that it screens transaction addresses using third-party risk data, including from Chainalysis, and an internal blocklist.

One Ethereum address received 2,804 ETH and 1.02 million USDT from Relay's router and solvers in 97 payments over about 80 minutes on Saturday, Etherscan data shows, matching SomaXBT's figures. The wallet swapped the USDT for ether on CoW Protocol and sent about 3,257 ETH, roughly $7.4 million, to four new addresses. None of the five addresses is on the FBI's list.

On Sunday, the hackers separately began swapping 970,522 SOL, worth about $95.9 million, for bitcoin through Relay, Lookonchain reported. The hackers' Solana wallet, the only Solana address on the FBI's list, moved 486,970 SOL ($46.4 million) in the hour before Lookonchain's 5:35 a.m. ET post. The Relay-powered swaps began after the FBI listed the wallet on Saturday. The wallet held about 466,700 SOL at publication time, the same balance as at 9:55 a.m. ET, per Solscan data.

Chainflip received 49.47 million USDT in 571 deposits, but many swaps failed, SomaXBT said. Failed swaps were refunded to fresh Tron wallets and sent back in, 17.91 million USDT in all. Chainflip planned an upgrade last year to block the Bybit hackers from its cross-chain DEX.

Chainflip said in a statement to The Block that it screens every deposit in real time against several anti-money laundering and blockchain analytics providers, whose lists include the addresses in the FBI alert, and rejects funds based on where they came from. Rejected deposits were refunded to fresh addresses that its providers did not flag as linked to the hack, so "when previously rejected funds were pushed back in from those addresses, some of them passed screening," said Shaun Janse van Vuuren, Chainflip’s head of growth and strategy.

Chainflip said it is working with its providers to tag refund addresses as linked to the original source immediately, a change it said has closed the workaround.

Symbiosis said early Sunday it had identified attempts to move Binance hack funds through its protocol and was in contact with Binance. "Our screening is built for normal flows, not for tracking fast-moving, sophisticated attempts so some mechanisms have gaps," Symbiosis said on X. "We're closing them as we go."

The attackers sent 49.71 million TRX into Symbiosis in 1,367 smaller deposits, SomaXBT said. Symbiosis recovered 15 BTC after an exploit of its own bitcoin bridge in September.

The hackers' main Tron distribution wallet paid out every hour for 31 straight hours and never paused for longer than 46 minutes, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said on Saturday. The same swap amounts kept recurring in THORChain deposits, one of them 19 times.

When a bridge rejected deposits, new wallets automatically re-sent the funds to the same destination, Elliptic said. In the Bybit case, laundering followed human working patterns, according to the firm.

Elliptic co-founder Tom Robinson said in comments shared with The Block that the activity does not appear to involve AI agents. "The pattern is repetitive and static: the same sizes, the same rhythm, the same routes, hour after hour," Robinson said. He added that test transactions and round-number top-ups point to "operators making decisions, with scripts doing the repetitive work."

Elliptic has verified $2.85 billion of the stolen funds as frozen or seized, about 44% of the $6.43 billion it counts as stolen, and 94% of that is stablecoins. No funds have been frozen on Bitcoin, the XRP Ledger, Solana or NEAR. About $3.25 billion, including 18,327 BTC and 233 million XRP, is held in assets that no issuer can freeze, the firm said.

Tether's frozen USDT is split across two attacker wallets, with 312.7 million in one and 65.99 million in the other, per Tronscan data. Mempool.space data checked by The Block shows all 18,270 BTC still sitting in the 19 bitcoin addresses on the FBI's list.

Chainalysis said on Saturday the hackers have been depositing stablecoins into DeFi protocols on Tron for depository receipt tokens, which cannot be frozen, and later redeeming them from new addresses. It did not name the protocol, which other onchain analysts identified as JustLend, and did not address a question from The Block about whether it was JustLend.

TRM Labs said 300 million USDT moved to a Tron wallet that "began supplying it to the JustLend lending protocol." Tronscan data shows that wallet put 10,000 USDT into JustLend, swapped about 234 million USDT for TRX on decentralized exchanges and sent 65.99 million USDT to one of the two frozen wallets.

The Block has reached out to Relay and Bitget Wallet for comment.

Updated on Nov. 2 at 10:40 a.m. ET with statements from Chainflip and Chad Barraford.
